This approach makes sense: match protocol-defined fields exactly while preserving the existing `DefaultOptions` behavior for user-defined data. I checked TypeScript, Python, Go, Rust, and Ruby. None binds `params.Name` as the canonical tool name, and canonical `name` wins when both spellings are present, regardless of order. TypeScript and Python runtime probes confirmed this in both protocol eras. This supports the change here. The important distinction is exact matching, not blanket rejection of noncanonical JSON. Peers differ in required-field validation, defaults, and raw/custom-result handling. Looks good overall. A few non-blocking suggestions: - Add a client-side result test covering alternate-cased optional fields such as `Content` and `IsError`, and a nested user-DTO-through-tool test confirming that its existing binding behavior is preserved. - Track the remaining internal casing differences separately, particularly task-based `CallToolResult` deserialization and transport-level `JsonRpcErrorDetail` parsing. These do not bypass the tool-name fix. - Include the behavior change in the planned minor-release notes. The shared context also changes OAuth model parsing, so that compatibility impact should be mentioned. CC @jeffhandley @halter73 Use caller-aware contracts for icon and annotation writes `src/​ModelContextProtocol.Core/​Protocol/​ContentBlock.cs:199` Nested reads now honor caller-modified contracts, but writes still use the SDK contracts at lines 384 and 421. With the new test's `src` → `callerSource` modifier, serializing a resource link as `ContentBlock` writes `src`, then reading it with the same options throws because the required `callerSource` property is missing. Resolve both icon and annotation write contracts through the same caller-aware fallback as reads, and add a round-trip regression test.
